item.title: Oleshky — new details on the Oct 27 deal:
item.description:
Reuters, CNN and The Times have now filled in the diplomacy behind the local ceasefire reported in the morning brief.
The deal was brokered with US First Lady Melania Trump acting as what her office calls the "exclusive intermediary," working directly with Ukrainian and Russian leadership; she said Oleshky's remaining 1,700–2,000 residents are mostly elderly in urgent need of medicine, food and clean water, with 30–50 children also thought to be in the town, and that residents who evacuate will get transport to their preferred destination — "some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine." Newsmax says it was granted exclusive TV access to document the operation.
On the wider war, Zelensky said technical-level talks with Russia and the US are set for the first half of November in Abu Dhabi, while a US official later said the next round could be in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland within a couple of weeks. The Oct 27 vs Oct 29 start-date dispute flagged in the morning brief is still unresolved.
Sources:
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Hormuz — the oil paradox:
item.description:
Total oil flows actually reached 24.5 million barrels per day in the week ending Oct 18 — slightly above the 24.4 million pre-war average from Feb 22 — according to Kpler data reported by TuzaraPost, because Gulf producers rerouted exports around the strait via the Red Sea and other alternatives.
But traffic through the strait itself is a fraction of normal: about 20 ships a day versus 100+ before the war, with many running dark (transponders off). US Central Command's claim of about 400 merchant transits in the preceding week is far higher than Kpler's count — the gap itself is a measure of how murky the strait picture is.
The IRGC says the strait is closed; CENTCOM says it is open; both can be half-right at once when "open" means a trickle of dark ships. Source:
Source: tuzarapost.substack.com.

item.title: NVIDIA OpenShell — the agent sandbox runtime, trending:
item.description:
OpenShell, Nvidia's open-source runtime for running AI agents safely, hit GitHub trending on Saturday with about 18.7k stars.
It is Apache-2.0, written in Rust, latest release v0.1.5 (Oct 20). Each agent runs in its own kernel-enforced sandbox, every network connection passes a policy check before leaving the sandbox, agents never see real credentials (OpenShell injects them only into requests to approved endpoints), and risky policy changes get flagged by formal verification before a human approves them.
Why it matters: it is the practical answer to "let the agent do things, but not everything" — the same OpenShell name appeared in Nvidia's GTC Berlin reference architecture this week, but this is the runtime itself gaining traction. Sources:
Source: digisoulhub.com.

item.title: PHP2Shell — first confirmed break-in, Palo Alto affected, patch lag now the story:
item.description:
The flaw is no longer just a warning. Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 reports the first confirmed PHP2Shell compromise, at a European government body, carried out with an AI attack agent, according to Carthage Electronics' Oct 24 threat brief.
Palo Alto confirmed on Oct 24 that the flaws affect its PAN-OS and Panorama management interfaces (product impact rated 8.7, below the underlying PHP 9.2), with no malicious exploitation against its own products known so far — fixed hotfixes are dated Oct 26 (11.1.16-h4) and Oct 28 (12.2.4-h1), with Panorama versions still to be confirmed; until then, restrict management-interface access to trusted addresses only. Meanwhile the patch lag is measurable: more than 21,000 Danish websites still lacked PHP security updates as of Saturday, per Danish industry reporting via NordiskPost, with Denmark's Aula school platform and the Danish Meteorological Institute among precautionary shutdowns (Norway and Finland took similar precautions), and South Africa's Presidency website remained offline as a precaution, with a spokesperson telling Reuters there was no indication of a breach.
Cloudflare's Matthew Prince said exploitation attempts on Cloudflare's network rose from thousands before disclosure to millions after. Most of what researchers see is still scanning, not confirmed mass break-ins — but the first confirmed compromise means the window for "we'll patch Monday" is closing.
Sources:
Source: carthageelectronics.com.

item.title: HPE Aruba — eight CVSS 10.0 flaws, patch this weekend if you run Aruba gear:
item.description:
HPE's advisory HPESBNW05162 (Oct 22) patches 72 vulnerabilities in the ArubaOS systems running wireless networks, and eight carry the maximum CVSS score of 10.0 — authentication bypasses, command injection, SQL injection and buffer overflows letting an unauthenticated attacker run commands on AOS-8 and AOS-10 Mobility Conductors, Controllers, Gateways and Access Points, several via the PAPI access-point management protocol on UDP port 8211.

Aruba gear sits in a lot of schools, clinics, warehouses and offices, so this is a weekend-planning item, not a Monday item. Source:

item.title: Quest Diagnostics breach confirmed — patient records accessed, scope still unknown:
item.description:
Quest told the SEC (8-K filed Oct 22) that it learned on Oct 21 of unauthorised access to its Quanum Lab Services Manager platform, used by healthcare clients to order lab tests and retrieve results.
Its Oct 23 security notice confirmed protected health information and personally identifiable information were involved, including "personal information and patient records," but the company has not disclosed how many patients are affected, which data types were taken, or when the intrusion began. Clinics relying on Quanum LSM are being told to place orders on paper forms or through Quanum eLabs, per BleepingComputer reporting.
If your doctor sends samples to Quest, this is one to watch — not a reason to panic, but a reason to watch insurance statements and unexpected messages. Sources:
Source: techycluster.com.

item.title: LiteLLM shipped a malicious release — check if you pulled 1.107.0:
item.description:
LiteLLM disclosed on Oct 24 that a master key for its Agent Platform, committed to a public repository on May 27, 2026, sat unrevoked for 136 days and was used from Oct 10 to steal an org owner's GitHub token — ending with a malicious LiteLLM 1.107.0 published to PyPI, Docker Hub and GHCR on Oct 21.
The poisoned PyPI release was live for roughly 1 hour 45 minutes before quarantine; the container tags stayed poisoned for about two and a half hours. Anyone who installed LiteLLM 1.107.0 or pulled the affected container tags on Oct 21 should treat exposed inference keys (Anthropic, OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, Together AI and more, per the report) as compromised and rotate them.
Single-source disclosure report — treat the details as reported, but the remediation advice stands regardless. Source:
Source: dev.to.

item.title: Overnight, both sides hit each other's war machine — and Crimea went dark
item.description:
The overnight exchange was a mirror image: Ukraine says it struck three Russian defence-linked sites, Russia fired 126 drones at Ukraine, and occupied Crimea lost power after a substation attack in southern Russia. None of it touches the narrow Oleshky humanitarian deal, which is still stuck on its own start-date dispute.
The details, in order. According to Reuters, Ukraine's General Staff said its forces hit the Proton-Elektroteks plant in Oryol, the Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical complex in Tolyatti, and an aircraft at the Yeysk airfield in Krasnodar region during operations on October 23 and overnight into Saturday. Kyiv says Proton makes components for cruise and ballistic missiles, and that Tolyattikauchuk's synthetic rubber can go into solid rocket propellant. Tolyatti mayor Ilya Sukhikh confirmed damage at several industrial facilities but did not name them, and reported no deaths or injuries there in preliminary information. At Yeysk, local authorities confirmed an attack but said it caused only minor damage to two apartment buildings — a much smaller account than Kyiv's aircraft-hit claim, so the scale there is unresolved. Separately, Oryol governor Andrei Klychkov said three people were killed Friday in a Ukrainian missile strike on an unspecified civilian facility in the region; Ukraine's General Staff did not report casualties, and the reports do not establish whether the two accounts describe the same strike. Russia's Defence Ministry, for its part, said air defences destroyed 1,297 drones, one French-made SCALP cruise missile and four Ukrainian Neptune missiles over the previous 24 hours — a ministry tally, not an independently verified count.
Russia's overnight barrage, according to Ukraine's Air Force via Anadolu Agency, was 126 drones, of which 101 were shot down, with strikes recorded at 14 locations. In Kyiv, the city military administration said two people were injured after an attack damaged a private residential building in the Obolonskyi district. Kharkiv's mayor reported a drone strike on the city's Industrialnyi district. Russia's Defence Ministry said it struck a facility at the port of Chornomorsk in the Odesa region used for producing uncrewed surface vessels, and a dry-cargo ship it said was carrying supplies for Ukraine's armed forces. In Russia's Rostov region, governor Yury Slyusar said drone debris damaged a transformer substation in the settlement of Kalinin, leaving more than 170 homes without power, and one person was injured.
The Crimea blackout is the night's biggest infrastructure story. According to the Kyiv Independent, via monitoring channels and NASA FIRMS satellite imagery, an attack damaged the Taman substation in Russia's Krasnodar Krai, which supplies occupied Crimea through the Kerch Strait energy bridge. The monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported on the evening of October 23 that "the entire peninsula is without electricity." Sevastopol's Russian-installed governor, Mykhailo Razvozhaev, confirmed on Telegram that the city was without power "as a result of an enemy attack on energy infrastructure outside of Sevastopol." Local authorities later claimed power was restored in multiple cities, but the Crimean Wind channel reported renewed blackouts in Simferopol, Yalta and Alushta, and internet watchdog NetBlocks reported widespread internet outages across the peninsula. Ukraine has not commented on the Taman attack, and the Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the extent of the blackouts. A Kyiv-based outlet separately reported electricity and water restrictions imposed after the blackout, with Sevastopol trolleybus service temporarily suspended.
What each side argues has not moved, but the rhetoric sharpened overnight. In an ABC News interview reported Saturday morning, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the Trump administration's recent actions toward Kyiv as "not supportive," and repeated that Starlink and Starshield speed restrictions are still in effect and interceptor-missile supplies are still delayed — directly contradicting President Trump's claim that access was restored. Zelenskyy also took a swipe at US envoy Steve Witkoff, who recently praised Vladimir Putin as "a humanitarian." Separately, the Independent's live blog reports that US lawmakers have written to Elon Musk giving him until October 31 to answer five questions about his control over Ukraine's military communications, warning that personal control over a foreign country's military communications raises corporate-governance and disclosure questions. That letter is reported by the Independent's live blog, not yet confirmed in a standalone report, so treat it as developing. On the Black Sea thread from Friday night, Moldova has now strongly condemned the attack on the civilian vessel near Romania's territorial waters, saying it stands in solidarity with Romania, Ukraine and Azerbaijan and urging a halt to attacks on civilian shipping.
For ordinary people, the Oleshky question is still the one with a human clock on it. Both Kyiv and Moscow now say their forces will stop firing around Oleshky at 4 a.m. local time on October 27 — Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets told the Associated Press the truce starts Tuesday and lasts several days, beginning with demining, then aid deliveries and evacuations — while the White House statement still gives October 29. Until the aid operation itself confirms a date, the roughly 1,700–2,000 mostly elderly residents still there wait. And the Crimea blackout is a reminder that the energy war cuts both ways: Ukrainian cities have lived through this all month, and now Sevastopol, Yalta and Simferopol are reporting the same kind of night.
In short: no breakthrough, no general ceasefire — just a grinding exchange of strikes on defence plants, ports and power grids, a still-unresolved Starlink dispute now drawing congressional questions, and an Oleshky aid operation whose start date Kyiv and Moscow agree on but Washington does not. Watch for whether Crimea's power holds through the weekend, for any Musk response ahead of the October 31 letter deadline, and for which Oleshky date the convoys actually run on.

item.title: Another missile at Riyadh, and Brent crude tops $117
item.description:
Saturday morning brought another Houthi missile at the Saudi capital and another leg up in oil prices — the two threads of this crisis moving together, as they have all week.
The details first. According to the Saudi-led coalition, via TBS News and AFP, air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis toward Riyadh early on Saturday, after civil defence activated an early-warning system for residents in Riyadh, Najran and Wadi al-Dawasir. item.title: SafePay ransomware has hit 600+ organisations — and it destroys backups first
item.description:
Catch-up, not overnight news: a joint advisory (AA26-293A) from CISA, the FBI, the US Secret Service and German and UK law enforcement, released October 20, says SafePay has compromised at least 600 organisations across critical infrastructure sectors since August 2024, across North America, South America, Europe and Australia.
SafePay is unusual in running as a non-affiliate operation — no outside affiliates, tight operational control. Initial access comes through brute-forced VPN credentials (often via Mullvad VPN exit nodes), phished account profiles, and automated exploitation of five known CVEs on internet-facing devices, including CVE-2024-40711 (CVSS 9.8, Veeam Backup and Replication deserialization).
Once inside, it uses living-off-the-land tools (PsExec, WinRM, RDP), harvests credentials, exfiltrates with 7-Zip/WinRAR and Rclone — and then factory-resets NAS devices, deletes shadow copies and kills backup agent processes before encrypting, so victims have no recovery path. Mitigations: patch those five CVEs, enforce MFA on remote access, and keep backups isolated and offline.
Why it matters now: it was not in this week's briefs, and its backup-destruction playbook is the detail that changes incident planning.
Source: gbhackers.com.

item.title: A certificate authority quit the TLS business after its private keys turned out to be trivially guessable
item.description:
Catch-up: Indian CA eMudhra announced October 22 that its board has voluntarily withdrawn from the global SSL/TLS certificate business, after a researcher showed the private keys behind eight of its browser-trusted intermediate certificates were so weak they could be calculated from the public certificates — one key was literally the number 4, and researcher Scott Helme recovered all eight on a laptop in under a second.
The keys came from a flawed key-generation ceremony in April 2025; Google, Mozilla, Apple and Microsoft blocked the affected certificates between October 17 and 20, and fixes have shipped in Go, Python, Node.js, Java and major Linux distributions. eMudhra says no end-entity certificates were issued from the affected intermediates, its infrastructure was not compromised and no data was breached, and it will keep revocation services running until all issued certificates expire or are replaced — offering Sectigo-issued replacements. Software that never checks revocation remains exposed until updated.
Source: computerworld.com.

item.title: Diplomacy on paper, drones over Moscow, and a ship hit off Romania
item.description:
Friday evening's war news undercut the day's diplomacy in three directions at once: Ukrainian drones shut down Moscow's airports for the second time in two days, a likely Russian drone struck a cargo ship just outside Romanian waters, and Vladimir Putin publicly rejected the freeze-the-frontline idea that underpins the talks — all while the Oleshky humanitarian deal itself turned out to carry two different start dates.
The details, in order. According to Russia's aviation regulator Rosaviatsia, all four Moscow airports — Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo, Vnukovo and Zhukovsky — suspended arrivals and departures on Friday afternoon as air defences engaged drones approaching the capital, with restrictions published at 2:05 p.m. Moscow time. Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 17 drones were shot down heading toward the city that afternoon, on top of 155 he said targeted Moscow Oblast overnight. At Sheremetyevo, an air alert sounded and passengers were directed to shelters, and an unverified social-media image purported to show drone debris on the tarmac; the Kyiv Independent could not independently verify it. Flight trackers disagreed on the scale — one count put Sheremetyevo alone at 85 cancellations and 229 delays over the day, another put all four airports at 147 delays and 31 cancellations as of 2:31 p.m. — so treat any single tally as partial. An evacuation was also reported at the IQ-Quarter tower in Moscow City, which houses several Russian government ministries; TASS later said, citing emergency services, that alarm was false. The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) notes this was the second full closure of all four Moscow airports in two days, after a similar shutdown on October 22.
What each side argues has, if anything, hardened. Putin said on October 22 that occupied Ukraine is "the territory of historical Russia" while rejecting Zelenskyy's October 21 proposal to freeze the current frontline, according to ISW's summary of his remarks — invoking "Novorossiya," a claimed region that, on ISW's reading, stretches beyond the four illegally annexed oblasts to include Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Mykolaiv and Odesa. ISW's assessment, stated bluntly, is that Putin's remarks show the Kremlin is willing to negotiate only to accept Kyiv's surrender, not a compromise peace — that is ISW's analysis, not a neutral fact, and Moscow would frame its demands as security guarantees, not surrender terms. Zelenskyy's side, as reported Friday, is still holding the freeze-along-current-lines offer, plus demands for security guarantees and 10 years of army funding. Meanwhile the Starlink dispute stayed unresolved into the evening: ISW reports Ukrainian officials, including the General Staff and defence ministry sources, widely reported continued in-motion speed restrictions on Starlink and Starshield on October 23, with defence minister Serhii Sternenko calling the situation "ambiguous" — some units report resumption above the old limits, others still see dropouts at speeds around 100 mph, and there is, per a ministry source, "no confirmation" the restrictions have been lifted. That directly contradicts Thursday's claim that full access had been restored.
For ordinary people, the spillover is the story. Romanian president Nicusor Dan said on October 23 that an unspecified drone struck the Comoros-flagged cargo ship Khoryv near Romanian territorial waters — about 13 nautical miles off Constanta, just outside the 12-mile limit — calling it a consequence of "Russia's aggression against Ukraine"; European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen called it yet another "Russian escalation" in the Black Sea. Moldovan police separately reported drone debris falling up to 100 meters from a residential building near Chistelnica on October 23. ISW notes this follows likely Russian strikes on two tankers inside Romanian waters on October 14–15 and on civilian vessels in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone on October 12–13 — a pattern, in ISW's view, of growing willingness to hit targets that touch NATO or NATO-aligned territory. And the Oleshky date gap matters for the 1,700–2,000 mostly elderly people still there: Gerasimov said Russian forces would cease fire on the Kherson axis from 4 a.m. Moscow time on October 27, while the White House release — and Melania Trump's own statement — put the localized ceasefire's start on October 29. Until one date is confirmed by the aid operation itself, the evacuation timetable is uncertain.
In short: Friday's talks window and prisoner swap are real, but Putin's own words point away from a frontline freeze, the Starlink limits are still reported in place, and the war disrupted Moscow air travel and Black Sea shipping on the same day. Watch for which Oleshky date the aid convoys actually run on, for any verified change in Starlink speeds, and for whether the Black Sea strikes draw a NATO response beyond statements.
Source: understandingwar.org.

item.title: Washington pulls its people out as October becomes the worst month on the water
item.description:
The sharpest Friday-night development on the Gulf front is not a new strike but a withdrawal: the United States has ordered non-emergency government staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, and Canada has added Dammam's airport to its avoid-all-travel list — while new Reuters data confirms October is already the worst month for Strait of Hormuz shipping attacks since records began.
The details first. According to NonRev Travel News' October 23 roundup, citing the State Department, spokesman Tommy Pigott said on X that non-emergency US government employees and family members must leave Saudi Arabia, citing Houthi attacks on civilian airports; the order applies to Saudi Arabia only, and Pigott called reports of a Gulf-wide order "inaccurate," though Reuters and AFP sources said families at some other Gulf posts are also being told to leave. The underlying reporting dates the order to October 22 — it was not in the evening brief, so it is reported here as a catch-up, not a Friday-night decision. Canada's travel advice, updated October 22, now says to avoid all travel to King Fahd International Airport in Dammam and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh because of military activity disrupting airport operations; the overall level is unchanged at avoid non-essential travel. On the ground, Riyadh's airport has resumed only a limited number of domestic flights on Saudia and flynas, subject to prior approval, with most foreign airlines still away — which settles the evening brief's open question in favour of "partly open, not really open." Saudi aviation authority GACA says Dammam resumed operations after Wednesday night's attack, which killed two people and injured eight.
On the fighting itself, ISW's October 23 Iran update reports Saudi air defences intercepted two ballistic missiles over Riyadh and Khamis Mushait and two drones over the southern region on October 23, in addition to a missile over Najran on October 22 — coalition-side claims, as usual, without independent confirmation of what was hit or missed. In Yemen, ISW also notes Yemeni government-aligned forces repelled Houthi attempts around Taiz City's "Old Airport" neighbourhood on October 22, after similar attempts on October 17–18, and that the Houthis fully encircled the city on October 12 — a reminder the ground war in Taiz is moving even as the air war dominates headlines.
The shipping numbers are the reason this is a major article, not just a travel notice. Reuters reported Friday, from Washington Institute fellow Noam Raydan's incident map, that October has seen 28 confirmed and reported attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waterways — the highest monthly number on record for a tracker running since 2017 — and 113 since the US-Israeli war with Iran began on February 28. The International Maritime Organization's tally broadly aligns at 120 incidents since the conflict began, with more than 30 supertankers (VLCCs) damaged, including 11 in October alone — about 3.5% of the entire global VLCC fleet. Greece-based consultancy Marisks adds that October 5–11 alone saw a dozen ships attacked, the highest weekly count of the war. Raydan's reading, via Reuters, is that Iran is intensifying attacks to slow the recovery in shipments and keep pressure on energy markets ahead of the November US midterms. Tehran's side of the argument is its claim of seven tankers hit overnight October 21–22, which President Trump publicly dismissed as fabricated, saying more oil is flowing through the Gulf than before the war; the claim remains unverified, with no vessel names given, and should not be counted as seven confirmed casualties. The US Central Command position, via Al Jazeera's reporting, is that about 95% of vessels are getting through.
For ordinary people, the costs are already concrete. Brent crude traded above $114 a barrel on Friday, a five-month peak, according to Reuters' market commentary — which is why fuel prices, not just headlines, are the transmission mechanism to watch. Airline suspensions now run deep into the calendar: Etihad and Qatar Airways suspended Riyadh and Dammam through October 24, Air France through October 24, KLM and SalamAir through October 31, Lufthansa Group through November 18 (Riyadh) and November 30 (Dammam), British Airways resuming one daily Riyadh flight only on November 3, Cathay Pacific out of Riyadh through January 31, 2027, and Delta's Atlanta–Riyadh launch postponed to March 2027. When the US pulls its own non-emergency staff, consular help for private travellers thins out too — the practical advice in the roundup is to postpone non-essential trips to Saudi Arabia.
In short: no newly verified Houthi hit on Friday night, but the US ordered departure, Canada's Dammam warning, and the record October shipping tally together say the Gulf crisis is deepening rather than stabilising. Watch for Egypt's parliament vote on military support on October 26, for any CENTCOM word on the claimed Sirik strike, and for whether Brent holds above $114 or retreats. No clean lead image could be retrieved from the Reuters or travel-roundup pages this evening, so this article runs without one rather than with a guessed image.
Source: nonrevtravelnews.com.

item.title: Wayve, Stellantis and Nvidia join France's government on an autonomous-vehicle push
item.description:
Announced October 23 at the Assises du Véhicule Autonome in Paris: Wayve's AI Driver, integrating Nvidia's Halos OS on Nvidia Hyperion compute and sensor architecture, combined with Stellantis' L4-Ready platforms and vehicle engineering, with the French government backing deployment in France and across the EU.
Wayve frames France — one of Europe's largest ride-hailing markets — as the base for a full autonomous-vehicle value chain, from chips to vehicles. Why it matters: this is a government-backed deployment pact, not just a tech demo, and it builds on existing Wayve–Stellantis–Nvidia collaborations.
Still an announcement, not cars on the road — watch for deployment dates.
Source: unite.ai.

item.title: OBS Studio 33.0.0 released October 23
item.description:
The free, open-source streaming and recording app's new stable release overhauls plugin loading (first-party plugins move to a new "core" folder; third-party plugins get a new location, with legacy locations still loading until version 34.0), improves source snapping in the preview with a new visual indicator, and runs on Windows 10+, macOS 13+ (Apple Silicon native) and Linux.
Why it matters: OBS is the default streaming tool for a huge share of creators, and a plugin-loading overhaul is the kind of change to check before upgrading mid-project.
Source: obs-versions.com.

item.title: Claude controls Photoshop via an open-source MCP server — unofficial
item.description:
An independent developer released a Photoshop MCP server on October 23 under an MIT licence on GitHub, letting Claude automate Photoshop tasks through natural-language commands via ExtendScript modules.
It needs Node.js 18+, a Claude API subscription and a licensed Photoshop copy. Flag: this is explicitly not affiliated with Anthropic or Adobe — a community project, not an official integration — so treat its roadmap (generative fill, batch processing) as aspirational.
Why it matters: it shows MCP moving from chatbots into professional creative tools.
Source: emergent.sh.

item.title: Nextcloud Collabora flaw joins CISA's exploited list — disabling the app does not protect you
item.description:
CISA added CVE-2026-110447 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 23, with a federal deadline of Monday, October 26.
The flaw is an unauthenticated command injection (CVSS 9.2) in Nextcloud's optional Collabora Online – Built-in CODE Server app (richdocumentscode); attackers have used it since September 10 to plant web shells and hunt for password vaults and crypto wallets, per the Carthage Electronics threat brief. The fix is version 26.4.303, and Collabora says simply disabling the app does *not* protect you.
Note: exploitation of this flaw was first reported October 15; the KEV listing and Monday deadline are what's new.
Source: carthageelectronics.com.

item.title: A local ceasefire, a talks date, and a prisoner swap — while the Starlink fight stays unresolved
item.description:
Friday produced the most concrete diplomatic movement in weeks, and it came in three pieces at once. According to Reuters, Ukraine and Russia said on Friday they had agreed on a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, brokered through US First Lady Melania Trump, and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said peace negotiators would meet next month for new talks. The two sides said the Oleshky ceasefire takes effect on October 27, allowing aid deliveries and civilian evacuations through humanitarian corridors. The White House said both nations agreed to temporarily stop all military action in Oleshky to allow aid in and prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway, and Russian chief of staff Valery Gerasimov said Russian troops would halt fire from 4 a.m. local time on October 27. Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets told Reuters the operation would involve demining roads to the town, delivering food and evacuating civilians.
The talks piece is now dated, if still soft. Zelenskyy said negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the United States had agreed to technical-level meetings in the first half of November in Abu Dhabi, and that he hoped a meeting of the countries' leaders would follow. A US official later told Reuters the three countries may hold their next talks in a couple of weeks in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland. Zelenskyy, speaking to the Hudson Institute via video link, said any peace agreement would need strong security guarantees for Ukraine and funding for 10 years to maintain the Ukrainian army, and stressed that Europe should also be involved. He also cautioned that much would depend on Russia, noting that a similar meeting expected this month had not materialised — a reminder that a talks date is not a talks outcome.
The arguments underneath have not moved. Zelenskyy is still holding the freeze-along-current-lines offer he made earlier in the week, while Moscow has only committed to talks after November 10, with the Donbas question — the gap between those two positions — untouched by Friday's announcements. And the third piece of Friday's news, a prisoner swap of 270 servicemen each, is the first since August, according to the Russian Defence Ministry; Zelenskyy called it a "very important result." Ukraine's acting prosecutor said on Telegram that more than 19,000 Ukrainian civilians, including 762 children, have been killed since Russia's full-scale invasion began, with 2,960 civilian deaths confirmed in 2026 alone.
The Starlink dispute, meanwhile, is now a direct contradiction rather than a misunderstanding. According to CNN, Ukrainian officials said on Friday morning that speed restrictions on Starlink and Starshield remain in place despite President Donald Trump's claim on Thursday that Elon Musk had restored full access. Trump told reporters on Friday that he had not spoken to Musk about the restrictions but would do so if required: "If there is a problem, I'll get it straightened out." Zelenskyy, speaking on Friday afternoon Kyiv time, said plainly: "The speed limits on Starlink and Starshield are still there, and the speed has not been restored." A Ukrainian Defence Ministry source told CNN there is "currently no confirmation that the restrictions have been lifted" and signal loss is still observed for ordnance travelling above 100 mph; one officer said connections drop for 10–15 seconds and "we lost a lot of assets, much more than usual." Musk has denied taking unilateral action, saying limits "are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS." Trump, pressed on who ordered the slowdown, said: "I have no idea, but I wouldn't tell you if I did." Zelenskyy also said Friday that delivery of already-agreed Patriot interceptors "is still delayed."
For ordinary Ukrainians, Friday's fighting did not pause for the diplomacy. According to CNN's tally of local officials, at least nine civilians were killed and 76 injured in the last day; Russia launched 176 attack drones on Thursday night and overnight; energy attacks in six regions left more than 500,000 people without power on Friday; and Sumy region saw strikes on civilian infrastructure and residential areas. In Russia, the defence ministry said it intercepted 443 Ukrainian drones overnight, with three civilians injured by falling debris in Nizhny Novgorod. Oleshky itself shows the human stakes of the local deal: the White House put its remaining population at 1,700–2,000, down from 24,000 before the war, mostly elderly residents needing medicine, food and clean water — and Melania Trump, who has been pressing the return of Ukrainian children seized by Russia, called it "a front-line war city on the brink of disaster." Pope Leo spoke to both Zelenskyy and Putin about the town in the past week, per Reuters.
In short: Friday gave the war a dated talks window, a local humanitarian ceasefire and a prisoner swap — real movement, but all of it narrow, and none of it touching the Donbas disagreement or the Starlink and interceptor disputes that are shaping the fighting right now. Watch for whether the Oleshky ceasefire holds from October 27, for a confirmed Abu Dhabi venue and date, and for any actual change in Starlink speeds or interceptor deliveries. Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Poland: Tusk raises the Lviv history row with Zelenskyy
item.description:
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Friday he had spoken with Zelenskyy about the Lviv Regional Council's resolution designating next year as the Year of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and its commander Roman Shukhevych.
Tusk said Zelenskyy told him he would not support such moves and was "very dissatisfied" with what happened, and warned that "genocide cannot be justified under any circumstances" and that Ukraine would face problems with European integration if it does not respect Polish sensitivities over the Volhynia tragedy. item.title: Apple briefly retakes the world's most valuable company crown — on the Duo's launch day
item.description:
Apple overtook Nvidia as the world's most valuable company on Friday, riding the iPhone Duo's launch day to a record stock price. According to 9to5Mac, Apple traded above $351 per share, setting a new intraday record, with a market cap around $5.12 trillion. Seeking Alpha put the early-Friday figure at $349.55 and about $5.10 trillion, against Nvidia at about $5.06 trillion. Multiple outlets note the crown changed hands again during the same session — Nvidia has since moved back in front, per Business Today — and that the two companies sit within 1% of each other, so a fraction of a percent swings the ranking.
The arguments about what the flip means are already split. The rotation case, put by market coverage on Friday, is that Apple is up about 4% since October 6 while Nvidia has fallen about 11% from its October 6 record close, with the Nasdaq down 2.6% on Thursday in a broad AI-stock selloff — investors are questioning how much AI infrastructure spending customers can actually finance, and Apple, which is not spending heavily on AI data centres, benefits by contrast. The sceptical case is that this is the fifth time Apple has grabbed the crown from Nvidia, and it has rarely stuck: since the start of 2024 the top spot has changed hands roughly two dozen times, and only once, during the DeepSeek scare in January 2025, did Apple hold it into the spring.
For ordinary buyers, the Duo story from this morning stands: $1,999 and up, January waits for new online orders, and a Saturday 10 AM ET restock check in the Apple Store app. One new detail Friday: Apple's marketing chief Greg Joswiak told CNBC pre-orders were "off the charts" and pushed back on production-problem reports, saying Apple is in a normal production ramp; Morgan Stanley's supply-chain checks point to about 6.5 million Duo units produced in the second half of 2026 — a limited volume next to conventional premium iPhones.
In short: the crown is a snapshot of a market rotation, not a verdict on either company, and it will likely flip again before the weekend is out. Watch for whether Apple holds the lead at a weekly close, and for the Saturday restock check.
Source: 9to5mac.com.

item.title: Quest Diagnostics confirms patient data compromised in Quanum lab portal breach
item.description:
Quest Diagnostics, one of the largest US lab-testing companies, confirmed that patient records were exposed after unauthorised access to its Quanum Lab Services Manager (LSM), the portal doctors use to order tests and view results.
Quest learned of the access on Wednesday, October 21, disclosed it in an SEC filing Thursday, and says protected health information was taken, including "personal information and patient records" — but has not said how many patients are affected, what specific data was taken, when the access began, or whether a ransom was demanded. No group had claimed the attack as of Thursday afternoon, and Quest says the incident is unrelated to this week's PHP vulnerabilities.
It paused LSM access and, as a precaution, other tools including Essential Insights and LabHQ. This is Quest's second major breach since 2019, when a third-party billing hack exposed 11.9 million records.
Source: techcrunch.com.

item.title: Missiles over Kyiv, drones over Moscow — and a freeze offer still on the table
item.description:
The war's heaviest exchange in days kept rolling overnight, even as both sides kept talking about talks — and the clearest peace offer on the table is now a freeze, not a settlement. According to TBS News, reporting the October 22 overnight barrage in full on Friday morning, Russia fired at least 21 ballistic missiles at Kyiv in three waves, Ukraine sent 630 drones toward Moscow according to Russian officials, and the two sides still exchanged war dead (252 bodies handed over by Moscow, 25 by Kyiv, per Belarusian agency Belta). The fuller toll from that night, per regional officials cited by TBS: two killed and 36 injured in a strike on a market in Lozova, near Kharkiv; three killed in Zaporizhzhia; one more killed in Dnipropetrovsk; and a Russian "massive strike" on port infrastructure in the Odesa region and on vessels Russia says Ukraine's military uses.
Overnight into Friday, the energy war continued. According to an OSNT daily brief summarising the night of October 22–23, a DTEK thermal power station was struck and ceased electricity generation entirely — the latest in a campaign President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says has hit Ukrainian energy facilities more than 170 times since October 11. The same brief reports Ukrainian drones hit the 75th Arsenal military plant in Serpukhov, near Moscow, linked to Buk and S-300 air-defence systems — reported by open-source trackers matching explosion footage to the site, not yet confirmed by either government. Treat both overnight claims as developing.
The arguments about what a deal even looks like are now unusually public. Zelenskyy, in a Fox News interview on Wednesday, said he would accept a deal freezing the war along the current front line. "Yes, right now we have to freeze, and I think this is a real way to end this war," he said, adding that security guarantees could be discussed afterwards — while refusing to give up the Donbas, which he called "not fair." Russia's position, via Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov after US envoy Steve Witkoff's three-hour meeting with President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, is talks only after November 10, possibly in Abu Dhabi, with the "nuances" from the Oslo round not entirely satisfying Moscow. A source close to the Kremlin told TBS the US proposals included Ukraine ceding Donbas in return for a NATO security guarantee — single-source, unverified, and flatly at odds with Zelenskyy's stated red line. Putin, interviewed on Russian television, confirmed he will resume US-mediated talks next month, saying the aim was security for Russia, Ukraine and Europe.
The US-Ukraine rift over Starlink is still unresolved, and both sides are now saying opposite things about it. President Donald Trump told reporters SpaceX chief Elon Musk had restored Ukraine's Starlink access, declining to say whether he had called Musk. Zelenskyy, speaking alongside Finland's prime minister, said speed on Starlink systems had not been restored, and a person familiar with the issue told TBS the curbs largely remain in place, with some drone units reaching 200 kph but "no official explanation of what's going on." On air defence, the picture is similarly contested: the Times, citing Ukrainian media, reported Kyiv could no longer shoot down ballistic missiles after running out of Patriot interceptors, while Russian state agency TASS reported Ukraine's military admitted it had not intercepted any Russian ballistic missile — both are claims from interested parties, not verified counts.
For ordinary Ukrainians, the human impact is winter arriving on a grid that has been hit more than 170 times in under two weeks, with homes, a monastery, shops, cafes, a market and a port all in the latest strike lists. For ordinary Russians near Moscow, the exchange runs the other way: two people wounded near the capital by drones, and one death in Belgorod, per Russian officials.
In short: the fighting is getting heavier even as a concrete proposal — freeze where the lines are, argue about guarantees later — is on the table from Kyiv and a talks window after November 10 is on the table from Moscow. The gap between those two positions is Donbas, and nothing overnight closed it. Watch for a confirmed talks date and venue, for any resolution of the Starlink and Patriot disputes, and for whether the energy strikes pause before winter bites. No clean lead image could be retrieved from the Kyiv article pages this morning, so this article runs without one rather than with a guessed image.

item.content:encoded:
The war's heaviest exchange in days kept rolling overnight, even as both sides kept talking about talks — and the clearest peace offer on the table is now a freeze, not a settlement. According to TBS News, reporting the October 22 overnight barrage in full on Friday morning, Russia fired at least 21 ballistic missiles at Kyiv in three waves, Ukraine sent 630 drones toward Moscow according to Russian officials, and the two sides still exchanged war dead (252 bodies handed over by Moscow, 25 by Kyiv, per Belarusian agency Belta). The fuller toll from that night, per regional officials cited by TBS: two killed and 36 injured in a strike on a market in Lozova, near Kharkiv; three killed in Zaporizhzhia; one more killed in Dnipropetrovsk; and a Russian "massive strike" on port infrastructure in the Odesa region and on vessels Russia says Ukraine's military uses.

Overnight into Friday, the energy war continued. According to an OSNT daily brief summarising the night of October 22–23, a DTEK thermal power station was struck and ceased electricity generation entirely — the latest in a campaign President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says has hit Ukrainian energy facilities more than 170 times since October 11. The same brief reports Ukrainian drones hit the 75th Arsenal military plant in Serpukhov, near Moscow, linked to Buk and S-300 air-defence systems — reported by open-source trackers matching explosion footage to the site, not yet confirmed by either government. Treat both overnight claims as developing.

The arguments about what a deal even looks like are now unusually public. Zelenskyy, in a Fox News interview on Wednesday, said he would accept a deal freezing the war along the current front line. "Yes, right now we have to freeze, and I think this is a real way to end this war," he said, adding that security guarantees could be discussed afterwards — while refusing to give up the Donbas, which he called "not fair." Russia's position, via Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov after US envoy Steve Witkoff's three-hour meeting with President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, is talks only after November 10, possibly in Abu Dhabi, with the "nuances" from the Oslo round not entirely satisfying Moscow. A source close to the Kremlin told TBS the US proposals included Ukraine ceding Donbas in return for a NATO security guarantee — single-source, unverified, and flatly at odds with Zelenskyy's stated red line. Putin, interviewed on Russian television, confirmed he will resume US-mediated talks next month, saying the aim was security for Russia, Ukraine and Europe.

The US-Ukraine rift over Starlink is still unresolved, and both sides are now saying opposite things about it. President Donald Trump told reporters SpaceX chief Elon Musk had restored Ukraine's Starlink access, declining to say whether he had called Musk. Zelenskyy, speaking alongside Finland's prime minister, said speed on Starlink systems had not been restored, and a person familiar with the issue told TBS the curbs largely remain in place, with some drone units reaching 200 kph but "no official explanation of what's going on." On air defence, the picture is similarly contested: the Times, citing Ukrainian media, reported Kyiv could no longer shoot down ballistic missiles after running out of Patriot interceptors, while Russian state agency TASS reported Ukraine's military admitted it had not intercepted any Russian ballistic missile — both are claims from interested parties, not verified counts.

For ordinary Ukrainians, the human impact is winter arriving on a grid that has been hit more than 170 times in under two weeks, with homes, a monastery, shops, cafes, a market and a port all in the latest strike lists. For ordinary Russians near Moscow, the exchange runs the other way: two people wounded near the capital by drones, and one death in Belgorod, per Russian officials.

In short: the fighting is getting heavier even as a concrete proposal — freeze where the lines are, argue about guarantees later — is on the table from Kyiv and a talks window after November 10 is on the table from Moscow. The gap between those two positions is Donbas, and nothing overnight closed it. Watch for a confirmed talks date and venue, for any resolution of the Starlink and Patriot disputes, and for whether the energy strikes pause before winter bites. item.title: No strike before Israel's election, says its army chief — while the missiles over Saudi Arabia keep coming
item.description:
The most useful new voice on the reported post-midterm strike plan is a dissenting one from inside Israel's own military. According to the Times of Israel, citing Channel 13, Israel Defence Forces Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir said he does not currently see an operational need to strike Iran before next week's Knesset election on October 27. "We do not see any indications of a need to strike Iran before the election. If we determine that a strike on Iran is necessary, we will carry it out," Zamir was quoted as saying. That sits in direct tension with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's campaign line this week — that regime change in Iran is "the only way to end this" and his directive to the IDF, Mossad and security agencies to topple it — and with President Donald Trump saying the US "may do it a little bit further" after already inflicting significant damage on Iran. A Jerusalem Post report cited by All Israel News added that IDF sources dispute that preparations for an imminent attack, like those before the June 2025 strike, have even been ordered. None of this cancels the Times/NPR reporting of a planned early-November window, but it does mean the plan is contested inside Israel, not just in Tehran.
Overnight, the Saudi front did not pause for that debate. The National's live blog, updated Friday morning, reports coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki saying ballistic missiles launched toward Riyadh and Najran were intercepted overnight. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree, meanwhile, claimed four "qualitative" operations over the past 48 hours — the defence ministry in Riyadh, King Fahd airport in Dammam, Aramco in Yanbu and Abha airport — with direct hits and a fire at Yanbu, and said Saudi Arabia has launched more than 2,900 strikes on Yemen in 100 days, killing and wounding more than 562 people, mostly women and children. The Houthi casualty claim for Yemen is unverified, and the scale of any damage from the ministry claim remains unconfirmed, with Saudi reports emphasising interceptions. The Dammam airport death toll from Wednesday's attack has risen to two, per The National.
In the Strait of Hormuz, the fog has thickened rather than cleared. Iran's claim that seven tankers were damaged overnight — four set ablaze during ship-to-ship transfers, three immobilised by mines — still has no ship names, flags or casualty figures and no independent confirmation. Trump accused Tehran on Truth Social of fabricating hits, mines "and everything else" to drive up oil prices before the US midterms, claiming more oil is now moving through Hormuz than before the conflict. Separately, reports on Friday said an oil spill reached beaches in Umm Al Quwain in the UAE, with beaches closed and clean-up teams deployed — attributed to regional reporting, still developing, and a reminder that even unverified claims sit on top of real environmental damage. One tracker put December Brent at $114.47 on Friday, up from $113.17 on Thursday.
For ordinary people, the travel squeeze tightened again: Etihad extended its suspension of flights to Riyadh and Dammam until November 5, will run only daytime flights to Jeddah, and noted Dammam airport has reopened while Riyadh's remains closed. That is the practical shape of the war for Gulf residents and travellers: airports that open and close, flights that only run in daylight, and fuel prices that move on claims nobody can yet verify.
In short: the strike plan is real enough to be argued about at the top of Israel's military, but not so settled that its own chief of staff sees a pre-election need for it; the Houthi campaign grinds on regardless; and Hormuz remains a place where claims move markets faster than facts can catch up. Watch for Netanyahu's October 27 election, for any CENTCOM word on the claimed Sirik strike from Thursday, and for independent confirmation — or debunking — of the seven-tanker claim. No clean lead image could be retrieved from the live-blog pages this morning, so this article runs without one rather than with a guessed image.

item.title: Apple's first foldable goes on sale — and immediately sells out
item.description:
Apple's first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo, officially launched on Friday, October 23, in more than 70 countries — and for most people who did not pre-order, the launch is already over. According to MacRumors, pre-order deliveries are arriving, but supply is extremely tight: shipping estimates for newly placed orders slipped to January 25 within the first 30 minutes of pre-orders opening on October 16, Apple warned walk-in stock would be limited, and US stores are limiting purchases to two per customer. 9to5Mac reports lines formed worldwide overnight — 30–40 people at 4:15 AM in Las Vegas growing to 150+ — with Apple Store workers telling disappointed shoppers to check the Apple Store app on Saturday at 10 AM ET for restock details. In Sydney, the first store to sell the phones, a queue formed before the 8 AM opening; in Shanghai, buyers queued from 6 AM.
The details: the Duo starts at $1,999 for 256GB, rising to $2,199 (512GB), $2,599 (1TB) and $3,199 (2TB), in Star White and Night Sky. Walk-in purchases are possible in the US, UK, Canada, Australia, Mexico and several European countries, but reservation-only in France, China, Hong Kong, India, Japan, Malaysia, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and the UAE. Carrier credits soften the blow in the US — up to $1,200 at AT&T, $1,000 at T-Mobile and $840 at Verizon with eligible trade-in, spread over 24–36 months — and 28 more countries get the phone on October 30.
The arguments about the launch are already running. Apple's framing, via chief executive John Ternus — celebrating the launch in Austin, with marketing chief Greg Joswiak at Fifth Avenue in New York — is that this is a new category, not a Pro Max alternative, and the response has been "nothing short of extraordinary." The sceptical case, put by Bloomberg's Mark Gurman in his Power On newsletter on Friday, is that Apple made a "major mistake" starting pre-orders on October 16 knowing manufacturing constraints were severe, rather than waiting until it had more inventory. Loop Capital downgraded Apple to Hold on October 20, cutting its price target from $370 to $330, citing weaker confidence in an iPhone shipment recovery and rising memory costs as a margin risk.
For ordinary buyers, the human impact is simple: a $1,999-and-up phone that most walk-in shoppers will not get today, a January wait for new online orders, and a second chance on Saturday morning via the store app. For Apple, it is the first major launch test for Ternus, barely a month after he took over as chief executive, landing just before earnings.
In short: the Duo is real, it is selling, and it is sold out — the launch-day story is supply, not the device itself, and the first real verdict on the phone will come from the people who actually got one. Watch for Saturday's restock check, for first hands-on reviews from launch-day buyers, and for whether the January delivery window moves.
Source: images.macrumors.com.

item.title: MOSS-Image: a 5B open image model built for design work, not pretty pictures
item.description:
OpenMOSS and Mosi released MOSS-Image, a 5-billion-parameter diffusion transformer trained from scratch, with Apache 2.0 code.
It is aimed at design work: a frozen Qwen3.5-9B text encoder, prompts up to 4,096 tokens, and structured JSON layout input with bounding boxes so a headline and a product land where asked. QbitAI reports 1.3 million downloads in its first four days across Hugging Face mirrors, top of the site's text-to-image trending board, first among open-weight models on the LLTB text-rendering benchmark at 96.3% coverage, and second only to GPT Image 2 in a blind design eval at 1,698.70 Elo.
An 8-step distilled variant has already passed 75,000 downloads, with GGUF, INT8 and MLX builds alongside. Benchmark and download claims are from the secondary write-up, not independently verified.
Source: siliconnoon.com.

item.title: MiniMax M3.1-Flash weights published
item.description:
The model that went on MiniMax's API on October 19 has its weights on Hugging Face as of Friday morning: 428 billion parameters in total, 23 billion active per token, native text, image and video input, and a 1M-token context.
MiniMax's own card claims 73.7% on DeepSWE v1.1 — behind DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017 at 77.0, ahead of Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3 — with 61.7 on OSWorld 2.0 and 82.2 on CyberGym, all vendor-run numbers. The engineering note worth reading is serving: sparse attention through every layer, quantization-aware training inside the routed experts, and a draft head for speculative decoding, which is why the checkpoint lands near 220 GB.
The license is MiniMax's own, not Apache — read it before building a product on it.
Source: siliconnoon.com.

item.title: Plex2Shell and SiteGuard: federal patch deadline is TODAY
item.description:
The CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities deadlines for Plex Media Server CVE-2026-96654 and CVE-2026-96656, plus SiteGuard CVE-2026-106931, fall today, October 23.
The KEV listing itself was reported on October 20–21; today is the day the deadline bites. Attackers are exploiting the Plex2Shell chain to deploy crypto miners and proxy malware, per The Hacker News, and the fix is Plex Media Server 1.43.3.10861 or later — a patch that has existed since August, which means victims are unpatched installs, not zero-day victims.
The other Plex pair (CVE-2026-96652/96655) and Siemens Software Center CVE-2026-110936 are due November 3. If you run Plex exposed to the internet, patch today, don't wait for the deadline to pass.
Source: secnews.gr.

item.title: A second outlet confirms the post-midterm strike planning — and Tehran answers that it is ready for war or diplomacy
item.description:
The reported US-Israel plan for renewed strikes on Iran, covered in the evening brief from the New York Times, gained a second, independent confirmation on Thursday. According to NPR, a person briefed on US and Israeli war planning said the two countries are preparing a possible attack in early November, after the US midterm elections on November 3, with US forces being amassed in the region to be ready by then. The source added a detail the Times account did not: Israel had initially planned to strike in mid-October, about two weeks before Israel's own elections on October 27, but President Donald Trump objected.
The same source cautioned, as the Times reporting did, that the preparations could also be a pressure campaign to force a diplomatic deal — and that no strike has been publicly approved. The White House line remains that the US will not attack Iran before the midterms. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, meanwhile, is campaigning on a threat to topple Iran's regime, NPR notes, and told a rally this week that regime change is "the only way to end this."
Iran's answer came from Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who told Iranian state media on Thursday: "We are just as prepared for diplomacy as we are for war," adding that "any scenario is conceivable, including the possibility of an attack by the US and Israel." Iranian state media also quoted a security source warning that if Iranian officials or civilian infrastructure were attacked, Iran would retaliate against US interests in the region and against countries participating in the war — and the Revolutionary Guard has repeated its threat to target Gulf data centres and undersea cables. The Institute for the Study of War adds that Iran reportedly conducted more than 30 tests of medium-range solid-fuel Emad and Kheibar Shikan ballistic missiles on October 11, almost certainly in preparation for a possible renewed conflict.
For ordinary people, the cost of the war that is already happening — not just the one being planned — got a stark new measure on Thursday. NPR cites a new International Monetary Fund report saying disruptions to energy production, shipping, tourism and trade have delivered substantial shocks across the Gulf: Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar are all expected to see economies contract by around 16% this year, and Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are also in recession this year. The IMF warns that if the war continues and energy disruptions persist, oil will average $130 a barrel in 2027. That is the backdrop to Brent still sitting above $113 and US gasoline still above $4 a gallon.
In short: this is still a reported plan, not an order — but now two outlets, the Times and NPR, have independently described the same early-November window, and both Tehran and Washington are talking as if the decision point is real. Watch for any White House confirmation or denial beyond the pre-midterm pledge, for Netanyahu's election on October 27, and for whether the force buildup NPR describes becomes visible in the Gulf.
Source: understandingwar.org.

item.title: 630 drones at Moscow, a prisoner exchange — and still no trust in the talks
item.description:
Hours after Russia's 21-missile barrage on Kyiv, Ukraine answered with its own mass strike, and the two sides still managed a prisoner exchange — a combination that captures where this war is: talking about talks, fighting harder. According to the New York Post, citing Russian officials, Ukraine fired 630 drones toward Moscow overnight, with at least two people injured in the Russian capital, according to Mayor Sergei Sobyanin, and at least one death and one injury in the Belgorod region. Russia said its air defences intercepted more than 800 drones in total, per other reporting of the same exchange. The Associated Press, meanwhile, puts the Kyiv toll at one killed and 22 wounded in the capital itself, while Ukrainian officials put the wider toll at two killed and 34 injured across 12 regions, including five children — the difference is geography, not contradiction: the AP figure is Kyiv, the wider figure is nationwide.
Zelenskyy framed the Kyiv strike as deliberate, not incidental. According to the Post, he said at least three of the missiles carried cluster munitions, that the targets included Kyiv's historic centre, monastery buildings, homes, shops and cafes, and that "the choice of weapon was deliberate, the choice of target area was deliberate, and so was the intent to inflict as much loss and damage on civilians as possible." Russia has not publicly addressed the cluster-munition claim. Moscow's position, via Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov, remains talks only after November 10, possibly in Abu Dhabi, with major disagreements over Donetsk and NATO membership unresolved; Ushakov added that the "nuances" from the Oslo round "do not entirely satisfy" Moscow. Zelenskyy said he would support talks but added, "We'll see what happens this time," shortly before air-raid alerts sounded over Kyiv.
The one concrete, verifiable step in the other direction was the exchange of war dead: Moscow handed over 252 bodies and Ukraine handed over 25, according to Belarusian state agency Belta, as reported by the Times of Earth. Such exchanges have accompanied moves toward talks in the past, but they are not a ceasefire, and they did not stop either night's bombardment. No clean lead image could be retrieved from the Kyiv article pages tonight, so this article runs without one rather than with a guessed image.
For ordinary Ukrainians, the human impact is unchanged and grim: homes, a monastery, a hypermarket, a postal cargo facility and transport infrastructure hit across Kyiv's districts, with winter approaching and energy infrastructure already under repeated attack. For ordinary Russians near the border, the Belgorod casualty shows the exchange runs both ways.
In short: the retaliation was as large as the original strike, the exchange was real but small against that scale, and the talks date is still disputed — Moscow after November 10, Kyiv wanting early November. Watch for a confirmed talks date and venue, for any US response on the reported Patriot interceptor shortage, and for whether the drone exchanges escalate further before any meeting.
Source: nypost.com.

item.title: Cloudflare's security-audit skill tops GitHub Trending — an agent auditor that tries to disprove its own findings
item.description:
Cloudflare's open-source security-audit-skill turns a coding agent into a security auditor through a structured six-phase audit: reconnaissance mapping architecture and trust boundaries, coverage-led hunting by isolated agents, candidate validation where every finding goes to a fresh verifier whose job is to disprove it, structured output to findings.json, re-verification of source claims, and a final report.
Each finding ends as confirmed, needs_validation (with the exact unresolved fact, no severity assigned), or rejected. It had 38,827 GitHub stars on October 22, topped GitHub Trending that day with 2,979 new stars, and is MIT licensed.
Why it matters: it is the skill Cloudflare says seeded its own vulnerability-discovery harness, and the disproof step is exactly what most AI security tools skip.
Source: digisoulhub.com.

item.title: Fortinet patches critical flaws — but won't say what they are until November 10
item.description:
Fortinet released patches on October 22 for FortiOS, FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer (FortiOS 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.13, 7.2.14, and matching FortiManager/FortiAnalyzer builds; FortiMail and FortiAuthenticator patches followed on October 21) covering critical and high-severity flaws — but the CVE IDs and full advisories will not be published until November 10, nearly three weeks later.
Fortinet urges customers not to wait: patch internet-facing devices first, and if you cannot patch, restrict admin access to trusted IPs, keep FortiManager off the internet, and enforce MFA. WatchTowr's warning, quoted by Cybernews, is blunt: the flaws will be rapidly reverse-engineered from the patches and exploited in the wild, and three weeks without details gives attackers a head start.
No active exploitation has been reported yet.
Source: cybernews.com.

item.title: Oil above $113 as reports of a post-midterm US-Israel strike plan rattle markets
item.description:
Thursday's big new development in the Gulf was not a fresh missile — it was a report about what may come next, and markets reacted as if it were. According to the New York Times, reported Wednesday evening by the New York Post and UBS, US and Israeli officials have drawn up plans for a "short but intensive" operation against Iran to begin after the US midterm elections on November 3. President Donald Trump told reporters late Wednesday that "something one way or another" will "happen fairly soon" in Iran — while repeating his pledge, covered in earlier briefs, that there will be no US strikes on Iran before the midterms.
Brent crude rose 4% to $113.17 a barrel on Thursday, with West Texas Intermediate up 2.4% to $99.47, according to the Post's market roundup; earlier in the day Brent had traded around $112–112.68, near its five-month high. The Nasdaq fell 2.6% to 26,008.86, its worst day since June, with the S&P 500 down 1.21%, as traders weighed both the Iran headlines and worries about tech companies' AI spending. Meta and Tesla led tech lower despite strong earnings, and Nvidia fell 4.4% on the day.
The two sides of the strike-plan story frame it very differently. Washington's public line, via State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott, pushed back on one part of the speculation: he denied a report that the US is preparing to order federal employees at other Gulf embassies to leave, saying the departure order covers Saudi Arabia specifically because of Houthi attacks there. That order, issued Wednesday, covers non-emergency US government staff and families in Saudi Arabia. Iran, for its part, has warned through the Revolutionary Guard Navy that continued US provocations could trigger a wider response against American bases across the Middle East — a warning repeated in Thursday's coverage of its vessel claims. Market analysts split on what the price move means: CIBC's Rebecca Babin told clients that "continued kinetic activity and the risk of renewed escalation following the midterms are keeping a floor under prices," while other traders noted distillate inventories rose against expectations, arguing against a sustained rally without actual supply losses.
Thursday also brought firmer, grimmer numbers on the Saudi attacks already reported this morning. The death toll from Wednesday's attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam rose to two — a Saudi citizen and an Indian national — with eight injured, according to The National's live coverage and Asharq News reporting; the civil aviation authority said operations at the airport have since resumed. A separate drone attack on Aramco's Shaybah oil field killed two workers, a Filipino and a Nepali contractor, Saudi authorities said, though operations at the 1-million-barrel-a-day field were unaffected. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted four drones over Eastern Province on Wednesday night and four more over the Riyadh and Medina regions on Thursday, and Aramco told essential staff at its Dhahran headquarters to keep working from home. The Houthis, meanwhile, warned Saudi Arabia against targeting Yemeni tribes and vowed to keep striking deeper inside the kingdom until attacks on Yemen stop and the blockade is lifted; they claim more than 2,900 Saudi strikes over the past 100 days killed or wounded over 562 people, mostly women and children — a Houthi tally that has not been independently verified.
For ordinary people, the squeeze is already visible and not abstract. US national average gasoline prices have stayed stubbornly above $4 a gallon, the Post notes, and one analyst cited in the morning brief warned prices are unlikely to fall below $4 for gasoline and $6 for diesel before the midterms without clear de-escalation. The IMF now forecasts a 4.8% contraction for Gulf economies as the Iran war hits exports, according to The National's live blog, and US Energy Information Administration data cited in Thursday coverage showed Saudi crude supply at 5.97 million barrels a day in August, down from 8.24 million in July. The stakes of the Yanbu claim from this morning also became clearer Thursday: Yanbu is the Red Sea terminal of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, the main route for exporting crude without passing through the Strait of Hormuz — so an attack there threatens the workaround keeping Gulf oil moving, even if no barrels were lost this time.
In short: no new US strike has been ordered, and the post-midterm plan is a reported plan, not an announcement — but oil above $113, a stock selloff, and a US departure order from Saudi Arabia show how seriously markets are taking it. Watch for any White House confirmation or denial of the Times report, for whether other Gulf missions follow the Saudi departure order, and for any independent confirmation of the vessel and Yanbu claims.
Source: nypost.com.

item.title: "Humanitarian" row erupts as Kyiv's toll rises and its air defences run dry
item.description:
The overnight Kyiv barrage covered in the morning brief grew grimmer — and more politically charged — during Thursday. Updated Ukrainian figures put the toll at two killed and 34 injured across Kyiv and 12 regions, including five children, according to Ukrinform's newsletter and the Washington Examiner; three of the ballistic missiles fired at Kyiv carried cluster warheads, Zelenskyy said. The Times reports, citing Ukrainian media, that Kyiv was unable to shoot down any of the missiles after running out of interceptors for its US Patriot air-defence systems — a claim that, if true, explains the scale of the damage, but which has not been confirmed by Ukrainian officials or the US.
The political flashpoint was a word. US envoy Steve Witkoff, after meeting Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday and securing the release of detained American Stephen Hubbard, told Putin: "You are a humanitarian also, sir. I salute you, and I commend you." Zelenskyy answered on X on Thursday: "Three waves of ballistic missiles have been launched at Kyiv by Russian 'humanitarians' since yesterday evening. They used 21 missiles." Trump, asked about the remark in the Oval Office on Wednesday, said Witkoff could have meant it for the "particular purpose" of Hubbard's release and added, "I wouldn't say anything one way or the other." The UK, per Ukrinform, rejected the "humanitarian" characterization of Putin outright.
The arguments behind the row show the real divide. Zelenskyy, in an interview with podcaster Steven Bartlett that aired Thursday, said holding the current front lines would already be "a huge compromise," and argued: "Trump can bring Putin to the negotiating table very easily. The way President Trump talks about me, he needs to adopt that kind of rhetoric about Putin." He said Wednesday he would accept a deal freezing fighting at the current lines. Trump, earlier in the week, said it may be "time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine" and that Zelenskyy "should have had this war settled a long time ago." European commentary collected by Eurotopics was sceptical of the talks themselves: The Spectator argued Putin is "using this to play for time ahead of a winter in which he hopes to make substantial progress," while the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung argued recent US moves have left the Kremlin convinced it has "the greater staying power" and can play Washington and Europe off against each other. Moscow's position, via aide Yuri Ushakov, remains talks only after November 10, possibly in Abu Dhabi, focused on a post-war security system — with no ceasefire agreed and major disagreements over Donetsk and NATO membership unresolved.
For ordinary Ukrainians, the human impact is the same story sharpened: homes on both sides of one Kyiv resident were hit, windows blown out, a neighbour killed, in the words of residents quoted by The Times; shopping malls, a monastery, a railway station and metro infrastructure were damaged; and with winter approaching, each night of strikes on energy infrastructure raises the prospect of cold, dark weeks. Ukraine also says it sent over 600 drones toward Moscow overnight, with Moscow's mayor reporting two people wounded — the exchange continuing even as negotiators talk about talking.
In short: the talks are still not scheduled, the date is still disputed, and Thursday's row over a single word captured why Kyiv doubts Moscow's intent — while the reported exhaustion of Patriot interceptors, if confirmed, would be the most consequential military detail of the day. Watch for confirmation of the interceptor shortage, for any US response on resupply, and for a confirmed talks date and venue.
Source: i.guim.co.uk.

item.title: Nvidia's Berlin pitch: AI factories in a shipping container — and a warning about the money behind the boom
item.description:
At GTC Berlin, Nvidia's big announcement was less a chip than a building: DSX POD, a reference design for complete Vera Rubin AI factories built by partners in modular containers, integrated and validated before delivery. According to Futurum's analysis and a StorageNewsletter summary of Nvidia's release, the factory-built units cut deployment at a prepared site from six months to as little as 14 days, with 17 partners set to deliver from early 2027 — Bull, Dell, HPE, Lenovo, Schneider Electric and Vertiv among them. Alongside it came OpenShell, an agent-security layer, and Sentry, extending Nvidia's stack from silicon to the agent runtime. The pitch to Europe, in CEO Jensen Huang's framing, is that Europe can produce AI rather than simply consume it — though Futurum notes the binding constraint in Europe remains access to grid power, which a container does not solve.
The supply-chain side landed the same day: Nvidia formalised a strategic partnership with Samsung Electro-Mechanics, which will expand dedicated AI semiconductor packaging lines in Sejong and Busan for Nvidia's chip substrates, Aju Press reports — the first formal partnership of its kind between the two. TechTimes reports Nvidia also committed $1.1 billion to chip-testing firm KYEC and locked in six supply-chain agreements aimed at doubling testing capacity. LG Innotek, meanwhile, unveiled a 3-megapixel camera module and a Multi-modal Vision System built for Nvidia's open-source Holoscan Sensor Bridge, which routes sensor data straight to the GPU without passing through the CPU.
Huang's other Thursday headline cut the other way. Speaking to CNBC at GTC Berlin, he said demand from "neoclouds" — firms that rent out GPU capacity, like CoreWeave, Iren and Nebius — is "off the charts," but "what is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth," adding that Nvidia wants its chips treated as a "financeable asset" with residual value as an asset class. That landed on a day AI stocks sold off hard: Nvidia itself fell 4.4%, AMD 8.2% and Micron 6.3%, with CoreWeave down 10.3%, per the Post's market roundup — investors weighing whether the AI spending boom pays off. In short: Nvidia is selling speed (14-day factories) and supply security, while its own CEO concedes the customers buying it all are short of cash, not customers.
Source: futurumgroup.com.

item.title: Follow-up: US agencies issue urgent PHP2Shell alert — while the exploitation timeline still doesn't add up
item.description:

Ordinary users are not being told to stop using the web; this is a server-side patching emergency.
