item.title: Missiles over Kyiv hours after Moscow agreed to resume talks
item.description:
Overnight into Thursday, Russia launched a large combined missile and drone attack across 12 Ukrainian regions, with Kyiv as the main target — hours after Vladimir Putin agreed in principle to resume US-brokered trilateral talks. According to AP, the Kyiv strikes killed one person and injured 22, with fires in the Dniprovskyi district on the eastern bank of the Dnipro injuring six including a child; the Guardian's account puts the national toll at at least two killed and 22 wounded including four children, with later Ukrainian figures citing 34 injured across Kyiv and other regions. Tolls are still being updated, so treat the exact numbers as developing.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said 21 missiles were fired at Kyiv in three waves from Wednesday evening, and that the southern port city of Odesa was also badly hit. The targets reported across the capital included civilian houses, energy infrastructure, an ambulance station, office buildings, a monastery and the southern bridge over the Dnipro River. Zelenskyy argued the timing showed no real change in Moscow's attitude, thanked Western partners who acknowledged that, and called for stronger air defences, Patriot interceptors and more sanctions.
The diplomatic side is where the two accounts diverge. The Kremlin's version, via foreign-policy adviser Yuri Ushakov, is that Putin agreed "in principle" to resume trilateral negotiations involving Russia, the US and Ukraine after November 10 — a week after the US midterm elections — possibly in Abu Dhabi, focused on a post-war security system. Zelenskyy welcomed the prospect of talks but was openly cautious — "We'll see what happens this time," he said shortly before air raid alerts sounded across Kyiv — and he has been pushing for negotiator-level talks no later than early November, not mid-November. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, said a settlement is "closer than ever before" and signaled he will not impose new sanctions on Russia for now.
For ordinary Ukrainians, the practical meaning is grim and familiar: another night of air raids, another round of damage to the energy grid weeks before winter, and a peace process that keeps producing meeting dates while the missiles keep flying. Ukrainian officials believe Russia's immediate aim is to degrade energy infrastructure before the cold sets in, leaving millions without light and heat. One small sign of continued cooperation: Zelenskyy confirmed US intelligence early warnings of missile launches have resumed, though the White House has not reversed a slowdown affecting Starshield, the military version of Starlink that Ukraine says it needs to intercept drones and carry out mid-range strikes. Russia, for its part, said it shot down hundreds of Ukrainian drones overnight, and local authorities in Belgorod said one man was killed and another wounded there.
In short: Moscow said yes to talks after November 10, then bombarded Kyiv the same night. Kyiv wants talks sooner and doubts Moscow's intent; Washington says a deal is closer than ever and is holding off on new sanctions. The gap between the talking and the bombing is the story — watch for a confirmed date and venue, and for whether the next night is quieter.
Source: i.guim.co.uk.

item.title: Thursday's Gulf escalation: Houthi claims widen, Iran claims seven ships hit, oil tops $112
item.description:
Thursday morning brought a sharp new round of Gulf escalation on two fronts at once — and the markets moved immediately. Yemen's Houthis said they launched attacks on Saudi Arabia's defence ministry in Riyadh, Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu, and King Fahd International Airport in Dammam. Reuters, carrying the Houthi statement, notes there was no immediate Saudi confirmation of attacks in Riyadh and Yanbu — so treat those two targets as claimed, not confirmed. The Dammam airport attack itself was already confirmed Wednesday (one killed, eight injured); Thursday's claim extends the campaign to the defence ministry and the Red Sea oil terminal city of Yanbu.
At the same time, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Navy claimed seven vessels were hit near the Strait of Hormuz in the past 24 hours: four vessels allegedly involved in ship-to-ship oil transfers in the northern Gulf were struck and caught fire on Wednesday, and three more allegedly struck naval mines west of the strait. The IRGC also warned the US military that continued provocations could trigger a wider response against American bases across the Middle East. That seven-vessel figure has not been independently verified — maritime authorities had confirmed only two incidents in the relevant period, and one separately reported tanker strike near Oman had all crew safe. If the full claim were verified, it would be the largest single-day vessel toll since the Iran war began on February 28.
The two sides of this tell very different stories. Iran presents its actions as enforcement against "illegal" oil transfers and unauthorized routes, with vessels running dark treated as hostile. The US and Gulf states present it as an assault on commercial shipping and civilian infrastructure: Washington ordered non-emergency staff and families out of Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, and Reuters reports Gulf stock markets fell Thursday morning — Saudi Arabia's benchmark down 1.2% toward an eighth weekly decline, Aramco down 0.5%, Dubai down 0.8%, Abu Dhabi down 0.5% — as fresh Houthi strikes fueled fears of broader escalation. Riyadh says it has answered with strikes on missile launcher sites and intercepted many Houthi ballistic missiles.
For ordinary people, the impact is already at the pump and in the markets: Brent crude topped $112 a barrel early Thursday, up more than 2–3% on the day, near its five-month high, with WTI near $99–100. One US fuel-price analyst warned gasoline and diesel prices nationally are unlikely to fall below $4 and $6 per gallon respectively before the midterms until there is clear de-escalation between the US and Iran and between Russia and Ukraine. Shipping through the strait remains severely disrupted, with transit counts far below pre-crisis levels.
In short: the Houthis claim a wider target list, Iran claims its biggest shipping day yet, and neither claim is fully verified — but oil above $112 and falling Gulf markets show the world is pricing in escalation anyway. Watch for Saudi confirmation or denial of the Riyadh and Yanbu claims, independent confirmation of the seven vessels, and whether other Gulf US missions follow Wednesday's departure order.
Source: devdiscourse.blob.core.windows.net.

item.title: Google's SynthID Detector goes global — now checks rivals' AI watermarks too
item.description:
Google's SynthID Detector is now available globally at SynthID.com, and it can check uploaded images, audio and video against watermarks not just from Google but from partner companies including OpenAI, NVIDIA and Kakao, with Apple support described as coming soon.
Until now users could only check content via Gemini, limited to Google-made material. The catch, which Google itself states: a negative result is not proof content is human-made — it only covers SynthID partners' watermarks, not AI content in general.
Why it matters: one upload point for the most common watermarked AI media is genuinely useful for spotting synthetic content, but it is a watermark checker, not a general AI detector.

item.title: Judge orders Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion in privacy case — Meta will appeal
item.description:
A New Mexico judge on Wednesday ordered Meta to pay the state $25 billion, one of the largest state verdicts against a company in US history, in a case stemming from the Cambridge Analytica scandal. A Santa Fe jury had found in September that Meta misled New Mexico residents about its data collection practices and its efforts to limit harmful content, committing more than 43 million violations of the state's Unfair Practices Act. Each violation carried a potential penalty of up to $5,000; Judge Francis Mathew's filing first calculated the statutory maximum at $219.5 billion, then reduced it to $25 billion, plus 15% annual interest until paid.
The two sides frame the case very differently. New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez called it a warning to all of big tech, saying the state's evidence showed Meta "lied to its users, to consumers, and to people all over the world" about how much control they had over their profile information, and that the money would go to the state's education fund — "we may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years." Meta's chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney countered that the ruling "makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," calling the lawsuit "a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online," and said the company is confident it will prevail on appeal. Meta has argued New Mexico did not prove any consumer was actually misled, and that a multi-billion penalty would violate due process and excessive-fines protections.
Legal experts told Reuters on Thursday that Meta has a strong basis for getting the penalty slashed on appeal — most vulnerably, whether a violation counts even without proof a particular person saw a misrepresentation or relied on it to their detriment. The state had asked for $35–45 billion; Meta had argued for roughly $3.45 billion.
For ordinary people, the practical point is narrow but important: this is a civil penalty paid to the state, not a consumer payout — Facebook users get no money from this case (the separate $725 million consumer class-action settlement already closed its claim deadline). Any benefit to New Mexicans would come indirectly, through school funding, and only if the judgment survives appeal. Meta's shares actually rose ~2% on Wednesday, as investors had priced in a large penalty after the September verdict.
In short: a record $25 billion number, a certain appeal, and a legal fight over whether 43 million violations can stand without proof anyone saw the statements. Watch the appeal — the final number, if any, is likely to look very different.
Source: techcrunch.com.

item.description:

The US Embassy in Riyadh also issued a security alert warning of possible further Houthi attacks. This is the sharpest US step yet in the Saudi-Houthi escalation — a formal ordered departure, not just a travel warning.
Source: devdiscourse.com.

item.title: Putin agrees "in principle" to trilateral talks after Nov. 10 — but not at the leaders' table
item.description:
The readout from the Witkoff–Putin meeting finally landed this afternoon: Kremlin foreign-policy adviser Yuri Ushakov said Putin agreed "in principle" that trilateral US–Russia–Ukraine talks will continue after Nov. 10, focused on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends."
A US official added the talks would happen "at the technical level" — meaning Putin himself won't sit down with Trump or Zelensky. Both sides accepted the trilateral format (Ukraine in Oslo Tuesday, Russia in St. Petersburg today), and the US readout cited "progress" on a post-war economic plan and European security architecture.
The catch, per CNN: no indication Russia has budged on its maximalist positions — full Donbas, a shrunken Ukrainian military, no NATO. Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev separately said the US–Russia diesel deal goes ahead despite European criticism.
Source: cnn.com.

item.title: Zelensky: "freeze and stop" — he'd accept a deal that freezes the current front lines
item.description:
In a Fox & Friends interview Wednesday morning, Zelensky said yes to a peace deal that freezes the fighting where it stands, with Ukraine keeping "75% or more" of its territory: "Right now we have to freeze, and I think this is (the) real way to end this war.
We call it a ceasefire… freeze and stop." He called that the minimum needed from Russia, followed by US and European security guarantees so "the occupation will not return."
He drew a line at giving up the Donbas — "not fair" — and at any deal negotiated without Ukraine ("don't speak about us without us"). It's a notable shift from his long-held rejection of frozen conflicts, and it landed hours before Putin's own "in principle" answer.
Source: nypost.com.

item.title: Iran–US deadlock, stated plainly by both sides: no talks under blockade, no relief while ships are attacked
item.description:
Iranian President Pezeshkian said Wednesday the US "cannot expect dialogue" while imposing a blockade and issuing threats.
Foreign Minister Araghchi, in a Financial Times op-ed, said Iran would give diplomacy "another chance" if it sees "strong evidence of a sincere desire" for a just solution — and urged a return to the June Islamabad memorandum, under which Iran would reopen the strait and the US would lift the blockade, release frozen oil funds and remove sanctions. Washington isn't biting: Secretary of State Rubio told US media a deal would be "extremely difficult" and economic pressure continues until Iran stops targeting commercial shipping.
Indirect backchannels via Pakistan and Qatar are reportedly still active, but nothing is confirmed.
Source: military.com.

item.title: Google Cloud's Vera Rubin A5X instances go live — general availability in November, up to 960,000 Rubin GPUs planned
item.description:

General availability comes next month, with expansion to Europe planned, and Google Cloud says it plans to scale Vera Rubin infrastructure to as many as 960,000 GPUs across multiple sites (a stated plan, not installed capacity). WPP also demoed a creative-agent reference architecture on A5X with Nvidia Nemotron models and OpenShell, with multi-node workloads running on a single instance in initial tests.
Source: unite.ai.

item.title: PHP2Shell: emergency patches out today for two critical PHP flaws — NSA, FBI and CISA say patch now or take systems offline
item.description:
PHP released fixes Wednesday (8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35) for CVE-2026-109618 (RCE via out-of-memory corruption) and CVE-2026-109619 (RCE via stale global state), both CVSS 9.2, both allowing unauthenticated remote code execution.
The release was pulled forward a day after details leaked on Hacker News ahead of the planned Oct. 22 disclosure. Apache mod_php is at highest risk — PHP says a demonstrated exploit triggers before application code runs — but FPM, CGI, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed are also at risk.
NSA, FBI and CISA urged immediate patching or taking unpatched systems offline; Unit 42 counts 22.6M+ internet-exposed instances potentially vulnerable. Cloudflare says it is already seeing early attack attempts and has deployed WAF rules; watchTowr honeypots logged exploitation attempts; several European government sites went offline to patch.
CISA had not observed exploitation as of publication, and neither CVE is on KEV yet — but exploit code is circulating publicly, so this is a patch-now, not patch-soon, item.
Source: defenseone.com.

item.title: LiteLLM 1.107.0 was hijacked on PyPI for ~1¾ hours — a credential stealer in one of AI's most-used plumbing packages
item.description:
BerriAI confirmed its LiteLLM 1.107.0 release, published to PyPI and Docker on Wednesday, "contained compiled malware which steals credentials and loads remote-code execution tools."
Attackers used three engineers' GitHub accounts via apparently stolen GitHub CLI tokens, overrode branch protection, and built the release from a lookalike "Berri-AI" copy of the repo. Seven malicious wheels were live on PyPI 11:39–13:23 UTC; tainted Docker images (including latest) stayed up until 14:20 UTC.
The payload steals SSH keys, cloud credentials, CI/CD secrets, browser passwords and LLM provider keys, and runs on any Python startup — even without importing litellm. Wiz already observed stolen AWS credentials being validated from 16:20 UTC, consistent with LLMjacking.
If you installed or ran 1.107.0, rotate everything it could have touched; 1.106.2 and the release candidates are clean. This is LiteLLM's second hijack this year.
Source: docs.litellm.ai.

item.title: Witkoff met Putin in St. Petersburg for ~3 hours — and Russia released an American prisoner
item.description:
US envoy Steve Witkoff carried the Oslo framework to Vladimir Putin on Wednesday morning at Constantine Palace, pushing to reopen direct US–Russia–Ukraine trilateral talks.
The Kremlin said the talks lasted about three hours, with no immediate comment afterward from either side. One concrete outcome did emerge: Witkoff announced Russia released 74-year-old American prisoner Stephen Hubbard, detained for more than four years.
The agenda also covered Russia helping resolve the Iran war and potential Russian fertilizer exports to the US. Moscow, meanwhile, struck a cool tone in advance — Lavrov said Russia "does not expect a miracle" and will not make "political concessions."
Zelensky's line before the meeting: "Let's see what Putin has to say," and that much depends on whether Washington hears "something new from Russia today — about peace, rather than the continuation of the war."
Source: cnn.com.

Russia's defence ministry gave a different account: a drone-storage warehouse complex in Poltava, the Nivki substation in Kyiv, and a cargo ship carrying military cargo to Odesa.

item.title: Starshield row sharpens: WSJ says Musk ordered the slowdown; Rubio says it's Musk's call, not the White House's
item.description:
The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that Elon Musk ordered the speed slowdown on Starshield, Ukraine's military-grade Starlink service, after discussions with Trump and White House officials — one source said beforehand, two said in the days after.
On Wednesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said decisions on Ukraine's Starlink access are up to SpaceX and Musk, not the White House, calling it "governed by a private commercial contract" — an apparent shift from his earlier position that no one ordered a slowdown. Defence Secretary Hegseth said Tuesday the Pentagon "hasn't pulled anything back" and issued no directives.
Meanwhile the practical problem is unresolved: reporting says Ukrainian drones still cannot fly faster than 130 km/h without losing connection. Zelensky said Tuesday that US early warnings are working again; the Starshield question is separate and still open.
Source: 941theduke.com.
